content: Sunscreens are prescribed to help prevent sunburn and to mitigate the harmful effects of sun exposure, such as premature skin aging and the development of skin cancer. Sunscreens are available in various forms, including creams, lotions, gels, sticks, sprays, and lip balms. These products are intended for external use only and should never be ingested. Sunscreens should be applied to the skin between 30 minutes and 2 hours before exposure to sunlight. In general, they should be reapplied every 80 minutes if you are swimming or sweating heavily, or every 2 hours if you are not in water. Always follow the instructions provided on the product label carefully, and consult your pharmacist if you have any questions or need clarification. You should also seek advice from your pharmacist or doctor to determine the most suitable sunscreen product for your needs. The choice of sunscreen depends on factors such as your history of sunburn and tanning, your skin type, any medications you are taking, and the specific reasons for using sunscreen. It is important to select a product with an appropriate sun protection factor (SPF) for your skin. In most cases, an SPF greater than 30 is unnecessary and not recommended. If you are using sunscreen to prevent drug-induced photosensitivity reactions or ultraviolet-induced skin disorders, opt for a broad-spectrum product and consult your pharmacist for guidance. If you anticipate swimming or heavy sweating, choose a sunscreen labeled as waterproof or very water-resistant. For infants under 6 months of age, consult your doctor before using sunscreen. For children older than 6 months, use a sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30. Sunscreen should be applied generously to all exposed areas of the skin. For an average adult wearing a bathing suit, the recommended application amounts are as follows: Face and neck: 1 half-teaspoon portion Arms and shoulders: 1 half-teaspoon portion for each arm Torso: 1 half-teaspoon portion for the front and 1 half-teaspoon portion for the back Legs and tops of feet: 2 half-teaspoon portions for each leg Before using sunscreen, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to sunscreens, diuretics (commonly referred to as water pills), sulfonamides, oral diabetic medications, acetazolamide (Diamox), or any other drugs. Additionally, let them know about any topical medications you are currently using. If you forget to apply sunscreen and realize this while you are exposed to the sun, apply it as soon as possible. Sunscreens may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: Skin rash Irritation Store sunscreen in the original container it came in, ensuring it is tightly closed and kept out of reach of children. If you have any questions about sunscreens, do not hesitate to ask your pharmacist for more information.
